title: Werner's Theory
summary: The structural foundation of coordination chemistry explaining primary and secondary valencies.
body:
Alfred Werner's theory explains the fundamental structure of coordination complexes.

  • Primary Valency (Principal Valency): Ionisable, non-directional, satisfied by anions, and corresponds to the formal oxidation state of the central metal.
  • Secondary Valency (Auxiliary Valency): Non-ionisable, highly directional in space (determining geometry), satisfied by neutral molecules or anions, and corresponds to the coordination number of the central metal.
  • Coordination Sphere: The central metal and directly coordinated ligands enclosed in square brackets $[\dots]$. Species inside do not ionise in solution.
  • Ionisation Sphere: The ionisable species outside the square brackets that balance the electrical charge.

title: Ligands and Chelates
summary: Molecules or ions that donate electron pairs to central metals, and the enhanced stability of ring-forming chelates.
body:
Ligands are ions or neutral molecules with lone pairs that form coordinate covalent bonds with the central metal.

  • Monodentate: Single donor atom (e.g., $H_2O, NH_3, Cl^-$).
  • Bidentate: Two donor atoms (e.g., ethylenediamine $en$, oxalate $ox^{2-}$).
  • Polydentate: Three or more donor atoms (e.g., $EDTA^{4-}$ is hexadentate).
  • Ambidentate: Monodentate ligands with two different potential donor atoms (e.g., $NO_2^-, SCN^-, CN^-$).
  • Chelate Effect: Polydentate ligands forming a closed ring structure (chelate) with the metal ion result in complexes with enhanced thermodynamic stability, primarily driven by a positive entropy change ($\Delta S^\circ > 0$).

title: Coordination Number & Geometry
summary: The relationship between the number of ligand donor atoms and the spatial geometry of the complex.
body:
The Coordination Number (C.N.) is the total number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal.

  • C.N. = 2: Linear geometry (e.g., $[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+$).
  • C.N. = 4: Can be Tetrahedral ($sp^3$) or Square Planar ($dsp^2$).
  • C.N. = 6: Octahedral geometry, utilizing either inner $d$-orbitals ($d^2sp^3$) or outer $d$-orbitals ($sp^3d^2$).

title: IUPAC Nomenclature
summary: Systematic rules for naming coordination compounds.
body:
Naming rules for coordination entities:

  • Order: Cation is named first, followed by the anion.
  • Ligand Ordering: Ligands are named in strictly alphabetical order before the central metal. Multiplicative prefixes (di, tri) do not affect alphabetical order.
  • Anionic Ligands: End with the suffix '-ido' (e.g., chlorido, cyanido).
  • Neutral Ligands: Retain their common names with exceptions: $H_2O$ (aqua), $NH_3$ (ammine), $CO$ (carbonyl), $NO$ (nitrosyl).
  • Central Metal: In anionic complexes, the metal's Latin name takes the suffix '-ate' (e.g., ferrate, cuprate). In cationic/neutral complexes, the standard name is used.
  • Oxidation State: Designated by Roman numerals in parentheses (e.g., $(II), (III)$).

title: Isomerism in Complexes
summary: Compounds with the same formula but different structural connectivity or spatial arrangements.
body:
Isomerism in coordination compounds is divided into Structural Isomerism and Stereoisomerism.

Structural Isomerism: - Ionisation: Exchange of coordinated ligand with ionisable counter ion. - Hydrate: Water molecules swap between inner coordination sphere and outer crystal lattice. - Linkage: Arises in complexes with ambidentate ligands (e.g., $NO_2^-$ vs $ONO^-$). - Coordination: Interchange of ligands between complex cation and complex anion.

Stereoisomerism: - Geometrical: cis (adjacent) vs trans (opposite) in square planar and octahedral complexes. fac (facial) vs mer (meridional) in octahedral $[Ma_3b_3]$. - Optical: Non-superimposable mirror images (chiral enantiomers). Complex must lack a plane of symmetry. e.g., $cis-[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^+$ is optically active, while $trans-[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^+$ is optically inactive.

title: Valence Bond Theory (VBT)
summary: Explains bonding, geometry, and magnetic behaviour via atomic orbital hybridization.
body:
VBT involves the hybridization of metal orbitals to accept ligand electron pairs.

  • $sp^3$ (Tetrahedral): Occurs with weak field ligands or $d^{10}$ systems.
  • $dsp^2$ (Square Planar): Strong field ligands force pairing in $d^8$ configurations, vacating an inner $d$-orbital.
  • $d^2sp^3$ (Inner Orbital Octahedral): Low-spin, spin-paired complexes formed with strong field ligands.
  • $sp^3d^2$ (Outer Orbital Octahedral): High-spin, spin-free complexes formed with weak field ligands.
  • Magnetic Moment: $\mu_s = \sqrt{n(n + 2)}$ B.M., where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons.

title: Crystal Field Theory (CFT)
summary: Electrostatic approach explaining $d$-orbital splitting, color, and magnetic properties.
body:
CFT assumes electrostatic interactions between the metal and ligands, leading to the splitting of degenerate $d$-orbitals.

  • Octahedral Splitting ($\Delta_o$): $e_g$ set goes up by $+0.6\Delta_o$, $t_{2g}$ set goes down by $-0.4\Delta_o$.
  • Tetrahedral Splitting ($\Delta_t$): Splitting is inverted ($t_2$ up, $e$ down) and smaller: $\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$. Always high-spin.
  • Spectrochemical Series: Determines ligand splitting power ($I^- < Cl^- < F^- < H_2O < NH_3 < en < CN^- < CO$).
  • High vs Low Spin: If $\Delta_o < P$ (pairing energy), high-spin complexes form. If $\Delta_o > P$, low-spin complexes form.
  • CFSE: Crystal Field Stabilization Energy $= [-0.4 \cdot n(t_{2g}) + 0.6 \cdot n(e_g)]\Delta_o$.
  • Colour: Arises from $d-d$ electron transitions or Ligand-to-Metal Charge Transfer (LMCT).

title: Stability of Complexes
summary: Thermodynamic and kinetic factors governing complex formation.
body:
Complex stability is determined by formation constants.

  • Overall Stability Constant ($\beta_n$): Product of stepwise formation constants ($K_1 \times K_2 \times \dots \times K_n$). Higher $\beta_n$ means greater thermodynamic stability.
  • Charge-to-Radius Ratio: Higher formal oxidation state and smaller ionic radius enhance stability.
  • Ligand Basicity: Stronger Lewis bases form more stable complexes.
  • Chelate Effect: Multidentate ligands form far more stable complexes than monodentate analogues.
  • Irving-Williams Series: Order of stability for divalent $3d$ metals: $Mn^{2+} < Fe^{2+} < Co^{2+} < Ni^{2+} < Cu^{2+} > Zn^{2+}$.

title: Effective Atomic Number (EAN) Rule
summary: Complexes gain stability by achieving a noble gas electron configuration.
body:
Sidgwick proposed that complexes are most stable when the central metal acquires the closed-shell electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas (e.g., Kr 36, Xe 54).

  • Formula: $EAN = Z - O.S. + 2 \times C.N.$
  • $Z = $ Atomic number of central metal.
  • $O.S. = $ Oxidation state.
  • $C.N. = $ Coordination number (or number of ligands $\times$ denticity $\times$ 2 electrons).
  • Examples: $[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-} \implies 26 - 2 + (2 \times 6) = 36$ (Kr configuration). $[Ni(CO)_4] \implies 28 - 0 + (2 \times 4) = 36$.

title: Metal Carbonyls & Synergic Bonding
summary: Organometallic compounds featuring carbon monoxide ligands and dual-character bonding.
body:
Metal carbonyls involve a unique synergic (cooperative) bonding mechanism with $CO$ ligands.

  • $\sigma$-Donation: $CO$ lone pair donates into an empty metal hybrid orbital ($M \leftarrow C$).
  • $\pi$-Backbonding: Filled metal $d$-orbitals back-donate into empty $\pi^*$ antibonding orbitals of $CO$ ($M \rightarrow C$).
  • Effects: Synergic bonding strengthens and shortens the $M-C$ bond but weakens and lengthens the $C-O$ bond, lowering its IR stretching frequency ($\nu_{CO}$).
  • Examples: $[Fe(CO)_5]$ (trigonal bipyramidal), $[Ni(CO)_4]$ (tetrahedral).

title: Applications of Coordination Compounds
summary: Crucial roles in biology, medicine, metallurgy, and analytical chemistry.
body:
Coordination compounds have widespread practical applications:

  • Biological Systems: Haemoglobin ($Fe^{2+}$ complex), Chlorophyll ($Mg^{2+}$ complex), Vitamin $B_{12}$ ($Co^{3+}$ complex).
  • Medicine: Cisplatin ($cis-[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]$) is an anti-cancer drug. $EDTA$ is used to treat heavy metal poisoning (e.g., lead).
  • Metallurgy: Extraction of gold and silver via cyanide complexes (MacArthur-Forrest process). Purification of nickel via $[Ni(CO)_4]$ (Mond's process).
  • Analytical Chemistry: Detection of $Ni^{2+}$ using DMG (rosy-red complex), and $Fe^{3+}$ using $SCN^-$ (blood-red complex).
